dimension: Routing and cascading among language models under cost and capability constraints
citations_that_failed: FrugalGPT arXiv:2305.05176 "later TMLR 2024" — UNVERIFIED. The arXiv page carries no journal reference and no comments field; OpenReview and TMLR searches returned nothing. Other 2025/2026 papers cite it as "Chen et al., 2024", so a 2024 venue may exist, but the venue as stated could not be confirmed. The paper itself, authors and the "two orders of magnitude" fee claim are all verbatim correct.
FrugalGPT "cascades capped at length 3" — NOT in the abstract and not confirmable from the abstract page. Plausibly in the body; cited as if established.

Boubdir et al. arXiv:2311.17295 "GEM 2023, NeurIPS 2024 poster" — the arXiv comments field reads "Revised version of the paper accepted at GEM Workshop, EMNLP 2023". No NeurIPS 2024 record found. The substantive claim is correct: the paper states "it's recommended to run numerous permutations, ideally with N_perm >= 100", sweeps N_perm from 1 to 10k, reports instability plateauing above 100, and reports volatility for closely matched pairs (Dolly pairing).

arXiv:2603.02540 characterised as "the largest factor analysis available" — the paper is "A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities" (Haznitrama, Ardi, Oh), a neuropsychological benchmark paper (NeuroCognition). The factor analysis is a secondary analysis on Artificial Analysis leaderboard data. The numbers survive verbatim: "exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on performance data obtained from Artificial Analysis for 156 distinct LLMs", 10 benchmarks, "Parallel analysis indicated a single-factor solution", "This factor (PA1) accounted for 75% of the total variance". The framing does not.

ATLAS arXiv:2511.04689 "matches whole-bank ability from 41 of 5,600 items ... a 90% reduction" — two different results conflated. The abstract says "reduces the number of required items by up to 90%" (an upper bound across benchmarks) and separately "matches whole-bank ability estimates using only 41 items (0.157 MAE) on HellaSwag (5,600 items)", which is ~99.3%, not 90%. "Matches" is qualified by 0.157 MAE. Submission date is 26 Oct 2025 (v1), last revised 13 Jul 2026.

EmbedLLM arXiv:2410.02223 described as "the sparse-matrix version ... which does not require every participant to attempt every probe" — UNVERIFIED. Neither the abstract nor the ICLR 2025 proceedings entry uses "sparse" or describes incomplete correctness matrices. ICLR 2025 acceptance IS confirmed (proceedings.iclr.cc, poster 30322).

TrustJudge arXiv:2509.21117 "15.22% ... for a strong judge" — the 15.22% is the pre-intervention baseline ("Pairwise Transitivity inconsistency by 10.82% (from 15.22% to 4.40%)") measured with Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as judge. Calling that "a strong judge" overstates; it is a mid-size open-weight model, not a frontier judge.

arXiv:2609.17857 generalisation — the design is four OPEN-WEIGHT families (Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2, Yi 1.5). Every number quoted is exact (3.4-8.4pp same-family lift, FPS 0.067, 95% CI [0.053, 0.084], permutation p = 0.0002, 9,312 judgments, 55.4% AB/BA reversal, 18.5% of pairwise outcomes). Extending it to a frontier multi-vendor panel is extrapolation, not measurement.

arXiv:2502.00409 "does not mention decentralised routing at all" — an absence claim verified only from the abstract/listing page, not the full survey. It is also stale: a TMLR 2026 survey of routing AND cascading exists (arXiv:2603.04445, Moslem & Kelleher) and is not cited.

RouteLLM "routes to hit a target such as 90% of the strong model's quality" — the paper and the LMSYS blog headline use 95% of GPT-4 performance, not 90%. The ICLR 2025 title given in the dimension ("Learning to Route LLMs from Preference Data") is CORRECT and differs from the arXiv title ("with Preference Data") exactly as claimed; the transfer result "routers maintain their performance even when the strong and weak models are changed at test time" is verbatim in the abstract.
Oracle ceiling "12.0 to 27.8 points" — only +27.8pp is confirmed in arXiv:2608.12150's abstract. The 12.0 lower end was not located.
quantitative_errors: UniRoute's "excess risk bound" is materially weaker than presented. It is Proposition 2 (Section 5.3), a DETERMINISTIC discrepancy bound: E[R01(r~*)] - E[R01(r*)] <= E_x[max over test LLMs h and clusters k of Delta_k(x,h)], where Delta_k is |per-prompt error given cluster k minus the cluster-level error Psi*_k(h)|. It carries NO rate in the number of samples n and NO rate in the number of clusters K, it holds only "under a regularity condition on P" that the text never defines, and it presupposes a K-component latent mixture P(x,y) = sum_k pi_k P(x,y|z=k) under 0-1 loss. There is no sample-complexity bound at all on how many probe prompts are needed to estimate a newly joining model's error vector — which is the single number the founder's cold-start mechanism would need. The bound is also tight only when within-cluster error dispersion is small, i.e. it degrades precisely in the regime a difficulty-stratified falsification clustering would occupy. Presenting this as "optimality results he does not have" overstates what is proved.

arXiv:2609.30360 (Gharat, Karamchandani, Nair; NeurIPS 2026) is proposed as the published optimal form of the knockout mechanism while omitting its load-bearing assumption: the algorithm assumes a CONDORCET WINNER EXISTS (the authors verify this empirically on some datasets). The dimension's own strongest-disagreement evidence — 15.22% pairwise transitivity inconsistency (2509.21117) and 55.4% AB/BA reversal (2609.17857) — is evidence against exactly that assumption. The dimension cites both sides and never reconciles them.

The 75%-single-factor argument is computed on the wrong object for the conclusion drawn. The EFA runs over 10 BENCHMARK-LEVEL AGGREGATE scores for 156 models. Aggregate scores being near-collinear is fully compatible with large item-level complementarity, and the dimension's own citations prove the coexistence: 16-38% item-level disagreement among top frontier models (2602.11898, verified; the abstract's full range is 16-66%) and oracle complementarity of +27.8pp (2608.12150, verified). Aggregation destroys the very variance a per-claim router exploits, so 75% shared variance in aggregates cannot refute a per-claim positional hypothesis.

Unnamed dimensionality conflict between two cited factor analyses. arXiv:2603.02540 retains ONE factor over a 156x10 matrix; arXiv:2507.20208 (Maimon et al., "From Benchmarks to Skills: Low-Rank Factors for LLM Evaluation") retains EIGHT over a 60x44 matrix ("uncovered 8 latent dimensions": General NLU, Entailment & Bias, Long-document comprehension, Instruction following & generation, Domain QA, Social & ethical judgment, Precision & fidelity, Grad-level reasoning). The dimension uses the first to refute the strong positional hypothesis and the second only as weak-form support, without noting that they disagree on dimensionality and that the disagreement is largely an artefact of matrix granularity (10 aggregates vs 44 benchmarks). The 1322 vs 1316 Arena gap (6 points, Figure 1, "the models differ substantially in latent skill profiles") is verified exactly.

tinyBenchmarks "within about 2% error" is an AVERAGE, not a bound: the paper states "achieving average estimation error under 2%", Figure 1 says "within 1.9% of their true accuracy on all of MMLU (14K examples)", and the error analysis says "the estimation error never exceeds 4% (except for one LLM with extremely low performance)". The 14K denominator is verbatim correct.

Verified exactly, and worth recording as surviving: arXiv:2605.06350 v2 (Bouchard, "Is Escalation Worth It? On the Depth of LLM Cascades", v1 7 May 2026, v2 5 Oct 2026) — 8 models, 9 deferral scores, 5 benchmarks; two-model cascades "improve mean test-set accuracy over single-model selection by 2.1 to 8.2 percentage points"; "allowing more than two models does not improve mean test-set accuracy in 118 of 135 comparisons" and "adds at most 0.43 percentage points". arXiv:2609.38274 — "+0.80 pp (95% CI: [0.44, 1.16])" for C2-MAS with Stacking (75.52% vs Quality-Only 74.72%), and "On the remaining four benchmarks the teams are identical" out of 7, with +1.87pp mean on the 3 that differ and +0.31pp out-of-domain on 6 held-out benchmarks. arXiv:2608.12150 — 4 models, 3 benchmarks, 56,476 inferences, 7 budget levels (64 to 4,096 tokens), rankings reverse on all benchmarks at p < 0.01 (McNemar), +1.6 to +5.7pp within domain and -1.2pp on transfer, 14.1% of the oracle gap captured. arXiv:2502.08773 — ">30 unseen LLMs", two instantiations "relying on cluster-based routing and a learned cluster map respectively". arXiv:2509.11106 — "higher validity and less variance on MMLU with fifty times fewer items". arXiv:2502.14074 — ICML 2025 Spotlight, "round-robin tournaments combined with Bradley-Terry models of preference can produce more reliable rankings". arXiv:2603.28622 — the greedy-heuristic characterisation is verbatim: "They typically rely on greedy latency heuristics or global DAG planning that assumes cooperative peers", with Petals' trust model tabulated as "Best-effort (cooperative assumption)". arXiv:2605.30736 OrcaRouter exists as described (LinUCB contextual bandit, offline reward matrix from curated routing prompts, RouterArena score 72.08).
overstated_verdicts: UniRoute (arXiv:2502.08773) rated DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE is overstated against hard constraint 4 (no central coordinator) and internally contradicts the dimension's own closing paragraph, which concedes that decentralisation is absent from this whole literature. UniRoute requires (a) a central labelled training set of per-prompt correctness for the incumbent models, (b) a globally fixed cluster map obtained by K-means over prompt embeddings, and (c) a single router that selects ONE model per query. None of the three survives a server-free roster unmodified. The honest verdict is APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES, with the specific change being that the cluster map and the error-vector store must be replicated or gossiped rather than held centrally.

arXiv:2605.06350 rated DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE is overstated in a different way: its optimality conditions are defined on 0-1 accuracy per query with per-stage thresholds tuned on a labelled validation set. A falsification harness whose output is an attempted refutation has no such per-query accuracy label, so "the ratio of expected accuracy gain to expected downstream cost is equal across boundaries" is not a condition CDSFL can currently evaluate. The transfer is an analogy, not an instantiation.

The dimension's single strongest objection may be BACKWARDS. The paper's own counterfactual says deeper cascades help when the confidence score discriminates the CURRENT model's correct from incorrect answers, and the benefit vanishes when the score reflects query difficulty shared across models. The dimension asserts that a falsification harness's natural score is shared claim-hardness. But a refutation is checkable per attempt: whether THIS seat produced a verified refutation of THIS claim is a current-participant-specific signal, which is the case the paper says deeper cascades DO help. The dimension presents an assumption about which score CDSFL would use as if it were the paper's measurement about CDSFL. The objection should be restated conditionally: tiers 3+ pay only if the escalation signal is per-seat refutation success rather than claim hardness.

"The decentralised, server-free requirement is absent from all of it" is FALSIFIED, not merely unsupported. Two papers directly occupy that space (see missed mechanisms): DiSRouter (arXiv:2510.19208) is coordinator-free by construction, and Federate the Router (arXiv:2601.22318) learns routers from decentralised sparse evaluations with theory that federation reduces routing suboptimality.

"Nobody in this literature routes among participants for FALSIFICATION work specifically" survives but only narrowly, and the dimension does not notice how close the nearest work sits: AutoMix (arXiv:2310.12963, NeurIPS 2024) routes on few-shot SELF-VERIFICATION, i.e. the routed quantity is a verification judgement about an answer rather than the answer itself. The gap is narrower than claimed.

The judge-bias contradiction ("a tournament in which the participants judge each other does not measure capability alone") is sound in direction but its magnitudes are carried over from four mid-size open-weight families and a 70B judge to a frontier multi-vendor panel without stating the extrapolation.

missed_mechanisms.name: DiSRouter: distributed self-routing with no central router
missed_mechanisms.citation: Hang Zheng, Hongshen Xu, Yongkai Lin, Shuai Fan, Lu Chen, Kai Yu, "DiSRouter: Distributed Self-Routing for LLM Selections", arXiv:2510.19208 (v1 22 Oct 2025, v2 1 Mar 2026)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: This is the one hard constraint the dimension declared unmet by the entire field. A query traverses a network of LLM agents, "each independently deciding whether to answer or route to other agents", on "its own self-awareness, its ability to judge its competence", instilled by "a two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline". Its stated motivation is that a centralized router "can not fully understand the knowledge boundaries of different LLMs". No central coordinator, no global error matrix, no roster-size ceiling, and no participant permanently eliminated. It is simultaneously the strongest published match for constraint 4 and the strongest competitor to the founder's probe-then-tier design, because it replaces probing with self-assessment. It reports no numbers in the abstract, so the comparison is a design comparison, not yet a measured one.

missed_mechanisms.name: Federated router learning from sparse, decentralised evaluations
missed_mechanisms.citation: Baris Askin, Shivam Patel, Anupam Nayak, Andrea Vigano, Jiin Woo, Gauri Joshi, Carlee Joe-Wong, "Federate the Router: Learning Language Model Routers with Sparse and Decentralized Evaluations", arXiv:2601.22318 (29 Jan 2026)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the case the dimension says does not exist: participants hold "limited" local evaluation data covering "a restricted query distribution and a biased subset of model evaluations", with "non-uniform model coverage". It supports both a parametric MLP router and a nonparametric K-means router (so it is the decentralised cousin of UniRoute), reports that "federated collaboration improves the accuracy-cost frontier over client-local routers", and claims theory that "federated training reduces routing suboptimality". Whether a central aggregator remains is not stated in the abstract and must be checked before claiming full server-freedom.

missed_mechanisms.name: Swiss-system / Swiss-Wise Iterative Matchmaking (Swim) tournaments
missed_mechanisms.citation: Yi Xu, Laura Ruis, Tim Rocktaeschel, Robert Kirk, "Investigating Non-Transitivity in LLM-as-a-Judge", arXiv:2502.14074, ICML 2025 (Spotlight)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension cites this paper twice for the criticism and omits its remedy. Alongside round-robin plus Bradley-Terry it proposes Swim as "a more computationally efficient alternative". A Swiss system is the mechanism that satisfies both of the founder's constraints the knockout violates: nobody is ever eliminated, and the comparison count is far below full round-robin. Recommending round-robin as the only fix overstates the cost of compliance by a large factor. The AAAI-22 paper the dimension cites also carries unused direct evidence here: its baseline set includes an ELIMINATION TOURNAMENT alongside round-robin, both beaten by MaxIn-Elo's UCB candidate set with max-uncertainty pair selection (Yan, Du, Ru, Wang, Zhang, Chen, "Learning to Identify Top Elo Ratings: A Dueling Bandits Approach", AAAI-22 pp. 8797-8805, DOI 10.1609/aaai.v36i8.20860, arXiv:2201.04480). The dimension cites "AAAI-22" with no title or authors, which is the weakest citation in the set even though it checks out.

missed_mechanisms.name: AutoMix: POMDP router over few-shot self-verification
missed_mechanisms.citation: Pranjal Aggarwal, Aman Madaan, Ankit Anand et al., "AutoMix: Automatically Mixing Language Models", arXiv:2310.12963, NeurIPS 2024
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: It is the published answer to the exact objection the dimension raises against FrugalGPT ("Cold start is assumed away by the existence of a labelled training set"). AutoMix uses a "few-shot self-verification mechanism, which estimates the reliability of its own outputs without requiring extensive training", and "a POMDP based router that can effectively select an appropriately sized model, based on answer confidence". For falsification routing it is the closest structural analogue in the literature, because the routed signal is a verification judgement rather than an answer.

missed_mechanisms.name: C3PO: label-free cascade optimisation with a conformal cost guarantee
missed_mechanisms.citation: Antonios Valkanas, Soumyasundar Pal, Pavel Rumiantsev, Yingxue Zhang, Mark Coates, "C3PO: Optimized Large Language Model Cascades with Probabilistic Cost Constraints for Reasoning", arXiv:2511.07396 (10 Nov 2025)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: Minimises "regret with respect to the most powerful model" using only unlabeled model outputs, and uses conformal prediction to bound the probability that inference cost exceeds a user-specified budget, with claimed guarantees on cost control and generalisation error from small calibration sets. This is the distribution-free guarantee the dimension says the cascade literature lacks, and it removes the labelled-data precondition that makes FrugalGPT's verdict APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES. The abstract states no numeric bound values, so the form of the guarantee must be read from the body before relying on it.

missed_mechanisms.name: The current survey of routing AND cascading
missed_mechanisms.citation: Yasmin Moslem, John D. Kelleher, "Dynamic Model Routing and Cascading for Efficient LLM Inference: A Survey", arXiv:2603.04445, accepted TMLR 2026 (v1 23 Feb 2026, v3 30 Aug 2026)
missed_mechanisms.why_it_matters: The dimension's open-problems claim rests on the abstract of a February 2025 survey (arXiv:2502.00409, Varangot-Reille et al., last revised 21 Jul 2025). A TMLR 2026 survey now covers both halves of this dimension in one taxonomy (query difficulty, human preferences, clustering, uncertainty quantification, reinforcement learning, multimodality, cascading, classified by when decisions are made, what information they use, how they are computed) and names its open problem as routing that "generalize[s] across diverse architectures, modalities, and applications". Any statement about what the field has not yet asked should be made against this survey, not the 2025 one.

notes:
METHOD. Every arXiv identifier in the dimension was resolved against arxiv.org directly; where a quantitative claim sat in the body rather than the abstract I fetched the HTML rendering (arxiv.org/html or ar5iv) and asked for the exact sentence. 23 citations checked. Bash has no network in this sandbox and the arXiv Atom API returned HTTP 429, so all verification went through per-paper fetches. No files were modified.

HEADLINE. Zero fabricated citations. All 21 arXiv identifiers resolve to real papers with the stated authors, and the great majority of the quoted figures are verbatim correct, including every number in the two most load-bearing claims (118 of 135 and at most 0.43pp from arXiv:2605.06350; +0.80pp with 95% CI [0.44, 1.16] and 4 of 7 identical teams from arXiv:2609.38274). My own prior that identifiers like 2609.38274 were implausibly high for a single month was wrong and I record it as refuted: arXiv monthly volume now reaches that range.

THE THREE DEFECTS THAT CHANGE A DECISION.

1. The absence claim is false. The dimension's central structural finding — that decentralised, server-free routing is absent from the entire literature — is contradicted by DiSRouter (arXiv:2510.19208), which routes by per-agent self-assessment with no router at all, and by Federate the Router (arXiv:2601.22318), which learns routers from sparse decentralised per-client evaluations. Both are directly on the founder's hardest constraint. This matters most because it is the one place the dimension told the founder he was in open ground.

2. UniRoute's guarantee is weaker than advertised, and its verdict conflicts with constraint 4. Proposition 2 is a deterministic discrepancy bound with no rate in n or K, an undefined regularity condition, a latent-mixture assumption, and no probing sample complexity. Combined with the central labelled correctness matrix, the global K-means cluster map and the single-model-per-query output, DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE cannot stand; APPLICABLE_WITH_CHANGES is the honest grade.

3. The cascade-depth objection may point the wrong way. arXiv:2605.06350's own counterfactual is that depth pays when the escalation score tracks the CURRENT model's correctness and not shared query difficulty. In a falsification harness the natural per-escalation signal is whether this seat produced a verified refutation, which is current-participant-specific and checkable. The dimension asserted claim-hardness as the signal and inherited the paper's negative result from that assumption. Restated correctly, the paper gives the founder a design rule rather than a refutation: score escalation on per-seat refutation success, and tiers beyond 2 may earn their cost; score it on claim hardness and the measured result says they will not.

SMALLER CORRECTIONS. ATLAS's 90% and its 41-of-5,600 HellaSwag case are two different numbers presented as one (the latter is about 99%, and "matches" carries 0.157 MAE). The 75%-single-factor refutation is computed over 10 benchmark-level aggregates and cannot speak to item-level complementarity, which the dimension's own citations measure at 16-38% disagreement among frontier models and +27.8pp oracle headroom; it also silently conflicts with the 8 factors retained in arXiv:2507.20208. arXiv:2603.02540 is a neuropsychology benchmark paper, not a factor-analysis paper, though its figures are exact. The cost-aware dueling-bandit algorithm offered as the published optimal knockout assumes a Condorcet winner, which is precisely what the dimension's own non-transitivity evidence puts in doubt. Two venue errors: FrugalGPT's TMLR 2024 could not be confirmed anywhere, and Boubdir et al. is GEM Workshop at EMNLP 2023, not a NeurIPS 2024 poster. TrustJudge's 15.22% is a Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct baseline, not "a strong judge", and the judge-bias magnitudes come from four open-weight families, not frontier models.

WHAT I COULD NOT CHECK. Whether FrugalGPT's body caps cascades at 3; whether EmbedLLM's correctness matrix is genuinely sparse; whether the full text of arXiv:2502.00409 mentions decentralised routing anywhere beyond the abstract; the 12.0 lower end of the quoted oracle-ceiling range; and whether Federate the Router retains a central aggregator, which decides how much of constraint 4 it actually satisfies.
